growth_story.headline: Zimbabwe's income per person collapsed in the 2000s, rebounded after 2009, then stalled; in 2025 it was still 16.0 percent below its 1998 peak.
growth_story.arc: Income per person grew 1.1 percent a year in 1990–1999 and reached its peak in 1998. From 2000 to 2008 it shrank 8.1 percent a year, as land reform disrupted farming and the central bank printed money to cover the budget gap, ending in hyperinflation. Switching to the US dollar in 2009 stopped the money printing, and income per person grew 7.2 percent a year in 2009–2016, though almost all of that came in 2009–2012. Since 2017 growth has averaged 1.1 percent a year, as new money creation, drought, a cyclone in 2019 and the pandemic brought deep falls in 2019 and 2020 before a rebound. A new currency, the ZiG, in April 2024 and an end to central bank lending to the state have since brought prices under control. Even so, income per person in 2025 was still 16.0 percent below its 1998 peak, about where it first was in 1970.

threads.title: Land reform and hyperinflation
threads.text: The land reform program that began in 2000 cut farm output and shook business confidence. The central bank covered the budget gap by printing money, and hyperinflation followed. Income per person fell in every year but one from 2000 to 2008.

citations.title: Zimbabwe Country Growth and Jobs Report
citations.quote: The land reform program from 2000 disrupted agricultural production and investor confidence, widening the fiscal deficit.

citations.title: Zimbabwe Country Growth and Jobs Report
citations.quote: Rather than adjusting spending, the RBZ financed the gap through money creation.

citations.title: Zimbabwe Country Growth and Jobs Report
citations.quote: The combined effect resulted in hyperinflation peaking at an estimated 90,000 percent in 2008, collapsing real incomes, destroying savings, and contracting formal employment.

threads.title: Dollar stability, short-lived
threads.text: Using the US dollar from 2009 took away the central bank's power to print money and brought quick stability. Income per person grew fast from 2009 to 2012, then barely moved from 2013 to 2016. The World Bank says that opening did not last because the wider framework stayed fragile.

citations.title: Zimbabwe Country Growth and Jobs Report
citations.quote: Full dollarization in 2009 removed RBZ’s ability to print money.

citations.title: Zimbabwe Country Growth and Jobs Report
citations.quote: Previous episodes of stabilization in Zimbabwe (between 2009 and 2014) created similar openings that ultimately proved short-lived, as the underlying macroeconomic framework remained fragile

threads.title: Electronic dollars and new shocks
threads.text: A drought in 2015–16 and spending before the 2018 election widened the budget gap, while the central bank created electronic dollars that could not be turned into cash. Cyclone Idai in 2019 and the pandemic followed, and income per person fell 7.8 percent in 2019 and 9.3 percent in 2020.

citations.title: Zimbabwe Country Growth and Jobs Report
citations.quote: High spending pressures from a severe drought in 2015-16 and fiscal expansion ahead of the 2018 elections widened the fiscal deficit

citations.title: Zimbabwe Country Growth and Jobs Report
citations.quote: the RBZ began creating electronic dollar balances (“nostro dollars”) that were treated as equivalent to real US dollars but inconvertible into cash

citations.title: Zimbabwe Country Growth and Jobs Report
citations.quote: This period saw the cyclone Idai shock in 2019 and global COVID pandemic in 2020-2021.

threads.title: Rain-fed farming drives swings
threads.text: The economy leans heavily on rain-fed farming, so the weather moves growth from year to year. A drought in 2024 cut growth, and income per person slipped 0.1 percent. A strong maize and tobacco harvest in 2025 lifted it 6.1 percent.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Zimbabwe

threads.title: A new currency, old debts
threads.text: The ZiG, launched in April 2024, together with an end to central bank lending to the government and tight money, brought prices down quickly. But large debts to foreign lenders remain unpaid, and they keep low-cost loans out of reach.

since_last_year.text: Growth picked up and prices calmed. Income per person rose 6.1 percent in 2025 on a strong harvest and mining. In April 2026 the IMF approved a program that tracks the government's policies without lending money, and by October 2026 the government had met all of its end-June targets. Local currency inflation fell to single digits.

citations.quote: The SMP is intended to help Zimbabwe establish a credible track record of policy implementation

citations.title: IMF Management Approves Completion of the Second Review under Zimbabwe’s Staff-Monitored Program
citations.quote: All end-June quantitative targets, structural benchmarks, and continuous commitments were met.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe a solid recovery since 2021, but income per person grew only 1.1 percent a year over 2017–2025 and 0.9 percent a year over 2016–2025. In 2025 it was still 16.0 percent below its 1998 peak. Part of the gap is that the sources measure total output, which also grows as the population grows, and the deep falls in income per person in 2019 and 2020 still weigh on the average.
